newsitem.title: USA: Car safety advocates call for dual-inflation airbags.
newsitem.headline: Car safety advocates call for dual-inflation airbags.

text.p: Safety advocates asked the federal government on Thursday to require that dual-inflation airbags be fitted on cars to better protect passengers, especially children, from injury when the bags inflate.

While bags are credited with saving hundreds of lives over the years, some 30 children have also been killed by the rapid inflation of the bags -- at up to 200 miles an hour. Experts say small adults and frail older people are also at risk.
The advocates said they petitioned the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to require dual inflation bags to be installed on cars starting no later than fall, 1998.
Dual inflation bags inflate more slowly in low-speed crashes, which cause only minor or moderate injuries, but faster in life-threatening high speed crashes.
Public Citizen and the Centre for Auto Safety said that suppliers of such bags told them they could be ready to intall such bags on all cars within three years for $10-$20 per car.
"Suppliers are just waiing for manufacturers to place their orders," said Public Citizen president Joan Claybrook.

The NHTSA is now considering new standards for airbags which include using a slower rate of inflation and installing an on-off switch so drivers can deactivate the bags when children or small adults are in the passenger seat.

The NHTSA decision is likely to be an interim move until "smart" airbags" can be developed which will "sense" when a child or smaller person is in the passenger seat and automatically reduce the air bag's inflation rate accordingly.

But Public Citizen said that dual inflation bags were the best solution for the near future because they neither surrendered protection of adults in high-speed crashes nor children in low speed crashes.
They said de-powering would reduce safety for children and that such a move was appropriate only on a very temporary basis.
The NHTSA and safety advocates say, however, that parents with cars with passenger-side airbags can generally eliminate the risk to children by insisting they ride buckled up in the rear seat.
